title: How Alien Hand Syndrome Works
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck discuss alien hand syndrome, a neurological condition in which one hand acts involuntarily and purposelessly, often without the person's awareness. They cover its history (first described in 1909, recognized medically around 1972), its four hallmarks (limb feels foreign, disconnected when not watched, personified by the patient, confusion between voluntary and involuntary movement), and the brain basis: a lesion on the corpus callosum disrupting communication between the frontal lobe and motor strip, with a 2007 fMRI study; a parietal lobe variant causing hand levitation when eyes are closed; no cure and management tips. They also note its portrayal in film (Dr. Strangelove, Mad Love, The Addams Family) and close with listener mail, including haiku and a limerick.

segments.title: Opening banter and Dr. Strangelove
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about Stanley Kubrick's Dr. Strangelove, with Peter Sellers in three roles, and say the title character seems to have alien hand syndrome. Josh introduces the episode topic, written by Chuck.

segments.title: History and hallmarks of alien hand syndrome
segments.summary: The condition was first described by the Germans in 1909 and gained medical acceptance around 1972; fewer than fifty cases have been documented. The hosts describe how the hand moves purposefully and involuntarily, sometimes during sleep, and outline four hallmarks: the limb feels foreign, feels detached when not watched, patients confuse voluntary and involuntary movement, and the limb is often personified and named.

segments.title: Brain basis: corpus callosum and motor strip
segments.summary: Chuck explains that a lesion on the corpus callosum, the brain's communication bundle, disrupts messages between the frontal lobe and the motor strip. The motor strip keeps firing without frontal lobe direction, producing purposeless movement. Lateralization of brain function is briefly explained. There is no cure; it is considered more a nuisance than dangerous, and a 2007 fMRI study identified the motor strip as a center of activity.

segments.title: Parietal lobe variant and management
segments.summary: A variant tied to parietal lobe damage can cause the hand to levitate, especially with eyes closed, and it can make dressing difficult. Dominant versus non-dominant hand patterns are described. Patients manage with oven mitts, occupying the hand, or in severe cases tying the hand behind the back.

segments.title: Alien hand in film and TV
segments.summary: The hosts discuss depictions of the condition in movies, starting with Mad Love, where Peter Lorre plays a doctor who transplants a murderer's hands onto a lover's husband, and The Addams Family, where Thing acts with purposeful independence. They note Hollywood's interest exceeds medicine's.

segments.title: Listener mail and haiku
segments.summary: Hosts read listener emails, including haiku from Crystal Duqui of Texas, a Greek myths podcast suggestion from Andy, praise from Sandra Thompson of Irvine, California, and a limerick from Bob.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode with contact information for podcast email.
